**Notice:** *In this assignment, all the plot should have title, caption, and axis labels. *

1. Use the dataset by of covid 19 by WHO at https://covid19.who.int/WHO-COVID-19-global-data.csv. Find the three countries with the most numbers of deaths by Covid-19. 

Hint: 

-  Use `filter` to select the most current date 

-  Pipe with `arrange(-Cumulative_deaths)` to rank the data by the number of cumulative deaths



```{r top-deaths}
# Read the WHO file saved in the same folder as this R Markdown file.
covid <- read_csv("WHO-COVID-19-global-data.csv")
covid <- covid %>%
  mutate(Date_reported = as.Date(Date_reported))

latest_date <- max(covid$Date_reported, na.rm = TRUE)

top_deaths <- covid %>%
  filter(Date_reported == latest_date) %>%
  arrange(-Cumulative_deaths) %>%
  slice_head(n = 3) %>%
  select(Country, Cumulative_deaths)

knitr::kable(top_deaths, col.names = c("Country", "Cumulative deaths"),
             format.args = list(big.mark = ","))
```

The latest date in this course dataset is `r format(latest_date, "%B %d, %Y")`.
The three countries with the most reported deaths are
`r paste(top_deaths$Country, collapse = ", ")`.


2. Use `transition_reveal` to make a plot revealing the number of deaths in the three countries with the most numbers of deaths


```{r reveal-deaths}
deaths_plot <- covid %>%
  filter(Country %in% top_deaths$Country) %>%
  arrange(Country, Date_reported) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = Date_reported, y = Cumulative_deaths,
             color = Country, group = Country)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::comma) +
  labs(title = "Reported COVID-19 deaths in the three leading countries",
       subtitle = "Date: {frame_along}",
       x = "Date", y = "Cumulative reported deaths", color = "Country",
       caption = "Source: WHO, course dataset through September 7, 2022.") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom") +
  transition_reveal(Date_reported)

animate(deaths_plot, nframes = 80, fps = 10, end_pause = 12,
        width = 850, height = 500, units = "px", res = 96,
        renderer = gifski_renderer())
```

The United States has the highest cumulative number of reported deaths,
followed by Brazil and India at the end of this dataset.


3. Create the new variable (column) `death_per_cases` recording the number of deaths per cases (Hint: divide cumulative deaths by cumulative cases).  What are the three countries with the highest deaths per cases? 


```{r deaths-per-case}
# A ratio is undefined when no cases have been reported.
covid <- covid %>%
  mutate(death_per_cases = if_else(Cumulative_cases > 0,
                                   Cumulative_deaths / Cumulative_cases,
                                   NA_real_))

top_ratios <- covid %>%
  filter(Date_reported == latest_date, !is.na(death_per_cases)) %>%
  arrange(-death_per_cases) %>%
  slice_head(n = 3) %>%
  select(Country, Cumulative_deaths, Cumulative_cases, death_per_cases)

top_ratios %>%
  mutate(death_per_cases = scales::percent(death_per_cases, accuracy = 0.01)) %>%
  knitr::kable(col.names = c("Country", "Deaths", "Cases", "Deaths per case"),
               format.args = list(big.mark = ","))
```

On `r format(latest_date, "%B %d, %Y")`, the highest ratios are
`r paste(paste0(top_ratios$Country, " (", scales::percent(top_ratios$death_per_cases, accuracy = 0.01), ")"), collapse = ", ")`.
These ratios use reported deaths and reported cases. They are not the
percentage of the entire population that died.


4. Use `transition_reveal` to make a plot revealing the number of deaths per cases of the US, Italy and Mexico. 


```{r reveal-deaths-per-case}
ratio_plot <- covid %>%
  filter(Country %in% c("United States of America", "Italy", "Mexico"),
         !is.na(death_per_cases)) %>%
  arrange(Country, Date_reported) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = Date_reported, y = death_per_cases,
             color = Country, group = Country)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(title = "Reported COVID-19 deaths per reported case",
       subtitle = "Date: {frame_along}",
       x = "Date", y = "Cumulative deaths / cumulative cases",
       color = "Country",
       caption = "Source: WHO, through September 7, 2022. Ratios use reported cases.") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom") +
  transition_reveal(Date_reported)

animate(ratio_plot, nframes = 80, fps = 10, end_pause = 12,
        width = 850, height = 500, units = "px", res = 96,
        renderer = gifski_renderer())
```

The lines show how cumulative deaths per reported case changed over time
in the United States, Italy, and Mexico. Early ratios can change sharply
when there are only a few reported cases.


5. Import the following data https://raw.githubusercontent.com/owid/covid-19-data/master/public/data/vaccinations/vaccinations.csv
                      
Use `transition_reveal` to plot the total vaccinations per hundred by level of income. Hint: the levels of income are identified in the `location` variable. Put a short comment on the caption of the plot. 


```{r reveal-vaccinations}
vaccinations <- read_csv("vaccinations.csv")

income_vaccinations <- vaccinations %>%
  mutate(date = as.Date(date)) %>%
  filter(location %in% c("High income", "Upper middle income",
                         "Lower middle income", "Low income"),
         !is.na(total_vaccinations_per_hundred)) %>%
  arrange(location, date)

vaccination_plot <- income_vaccinations %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = date, y = total_vaccinations_per_hundred,
             color = location, group = location)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  labs(title = "COVID-19 vaccination doses by income group",
       subtitle = "Date: {frame_along}",
       x = "Date", y = "Total vaccination doses per 100 people",
       color = "Income group",
       caption = paste("Source: Our World in Data. Higher-income groups received more doses per 100 people.",
                       "Totals include multiple doses per person, so they can exceed 100.",
                       sep = "\n")) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom") +
  transition_reveal(date)

animate(vaccination_plot, nframes = 80, fps = 10, end_pause = 12,
        width = 900, height = 520, units = "px", res = 96,
        renderer = gifski_renderer())
```

This vaccination dataset covers a different period from the WHO course file.
The income-group observations used here run from
`r format(min(income_vaccinations$date), "%B %d, %Y")` to
`r format(max(income_vaccinations$date), "%B %d, %Y")`.
The graph counts doses per 100 people, not the percentage of people vaccinated.
